findings.why: The Day 1 / After 6 washes / Week 4 frames form a time-lapse of improvement set against the 6-wash and 4-week stats, and AI-generated frames are not representative, unretouched evidence (the "not real results" note sits only in the footnote). The headline repeats the same day-one-to-week-four timeline.
findings.fix: Relabel the frames as routine stages (e.g. "Week 4 · in the routine") with the AI-illustration note on the image itself, or replace them with real, unretouched study photos and their qualifier.

rule_hit_review.why: As an on-image frame caption it presents the 6-wash result as a visual milestone with no qualifier beside it; the underlying stat is F16.
Matches F16 and is perception-worded ("agreed"); acceptable if the study file confirms the 6-wash window and the footnote labels it a consumer perception study.
Matches F18 ("felt smoother & brighter after 4 weeks"); same condition as the 6-wash window.
Keeps "agreed", but "significant reduction in skin oiliness" can read as clinical significance; scope it as perception and add study type and n.
Matches F18 and is perception-worded ("felt"); it needs the study-type and n qualifier on the creative.

tone_read: Calm and data-led, with no fear hook, hype or exclamation. The day-one-to-week-four timeline leans toward category "transformation" creative rather than Minimalist's education-first voice.
language_read: "2% Salicylic Acid + LHA" and "Salicylic Acid + LHA 2% Cleanser" are in house format, and the stats keep "subjects agreed" wording. "Significant reduction in skin oiliness" is the page's phrase but reads stronger than the perception framing it sits in.
